segments.title: Arctic convoy cargo losses and political risk
segments.body: The extract turns Arctic convoy losses into a concrete logistics problem. It puts 77 aircraft, 147 tanks, and 717 military vehicles at the bottom of the Arctic Ocean, one quarter of the cargo. A few Luftwaffe aircraft destroyed in a day equipment that a brigade might have taken a month to eliminate in combat. After PQ 15, Home Fleet commander Sir John Tovey and Admiral Bonham-Carter argued that summer convoys should stop unless northern Norwegian airfields could be neutralized or darkness restored cover. Admiral Pound agreed that the strategic situation favored the enemy. If the convoys continued for political reasons, the admirals expected very heavy losses.

evidence.note: The reading quantifies lost aircraft, tanks, and vehicles, then gives Tovey, Bonham-Carter, and Pound's assessment of daylight convoy risk and political pressure to continue.

segments.summary: The Target Tirpitz extract measures the military cargo lost in one Arctic convoy attack and explains why commanders questioned summer sailings despite political pressure to continue them.

segments.title: Target Tirpitz and the Arctic convoy threat
segments.body: The book places attacks on Tirpitz within the problem of sustaining Arctic convoys to the Soviet Union. Official historian Stephen Roskill described the planning and execution of each convoy as a gamble that would eventually bring disaster. PQ 15, PQ 16, and PQ 17 appear as stages in that mounting crisis. Planners faced Luftwaffe aircraft from northern Norway, U-boats, and major German surface raiders at the same time. Tirpitz mattered because her threat complicated the balance among escorts, covering forces, and the other dangers facing every convoy.

evidence.note: PQ 15, PQ 16, and PQ 17 in relation to planners' expectation of disaster from the combined U-boat, aircraft, and surface-raider threat.

segments.summary: Patrick Bishop's Target Tirpitz shows planners expecting disaster as they balanced Luftwaffe aircraft, U-boats, and German surface raiders against the Arctic convoys.

segments.title: LRDG range depended on supply and forward basing
segments.body: The passage makes logistics the foundation of desert special operations. An LRDG patrol could remain away for three weeks and cover about two thousand miles. At only six miles per gallon, ten or more trucks might set out mainly to carry petrol, water, ammunition, and other supplies. That reach enabled raids on remote airfields and forts where Italian forces did not expect British raiders to appear. General Leclerc's Free French capture of Kufra gave the LRDG and SAS their main forward base. Fresh water, palm shade, and several days' rest made the oasis a practical source of endurance for further raids.

evidence.note: The reading details patrol range, fuel and water burdens, remote raids, the morale effect on Italian forces, and Kufra's value as an LRDG and SAS forward base.

segments.summary: The Long Range Desert Group's reach rested on truck capacity, tightly rationed water, and the Free French capture of Kufra as a forward base.

segments.title: How the Long Range Desert Group raided
segments.body: The account follows Captain Hay's G1 patrol after an Italian aircraft spotted it near the Benghazi road and called in a German Junkers 87. The patrol survived the bombing and strafing, hid overnight in a familiar wadi, and reconnoitred a vehicle park. At dusk it approached openly in British trucks, which German and Italian troops ignored because Axis forces commonly used captured vehicles. The raiders then concentrated machine-gun and anti-tank-rifle fire, threw grenades into the huts, and withdrew before the defenders could organize. They spent the next day hidden under camouflage, then attacked a petrol tanker that evening and returned without casualties. The closing comparison links this mix of mobility, firepower, support, and opportunism to the special forces support group used in Afghanistan and Iraq.

evidence.note: A patrol uses reconnaissance, disguise by familiarity, concentrated fire, withdrawal, and concealment to attack Axis road traffic without casualties.

segments.summary: John Laffin's Raiders follows an LRDG patrol using reconnaissance, familiar British trucks, concentrated fire, and concealed withdrawal against Axis road traffic.

segments.title: Forces converging on Pegasus Bridge
segments.body: Ambrose shifts from the assault plan to the people whose paths were converging on the bridge in early 1944. Two German recruits arrive in the 716th Infantry Division after different journeys through wartime Europe, while a French family at the nearby café continues civilian life under occupation. A German parachute regiment returns from fighting at Salerno and Cassino to rebuild and train near Bologna. These men join John Howard's company and von Luck's 21st Panzer Division in winter training for battles they cannot yet fully foresee. Pegasus Bridge becomes a meeting point for occupation troops, combat veterans, civilians, and an airborne assault force.

evidence.note: The reading traces German recruits, a veteran parachute regiment, nearby French civilians, Howard's company, and 21st Panzer through the winter training that precedes the Normandy battle.

segments.summary: Ambrose follows German coastal troops, veteran paratroopers, French civilians, John Howard's company, and 21st Panzer as their paths converge around Pegasus Bridge.

segments.title: Glider lessons behind the Pegasus Bridge assault
segments.body: The extract opens with British glider pilots' dislike of the American Waco, which carried only thirteen men, landed on skids, and was difficult to handle. During the invasion of Sicily, the Dakota tugs lacked self-sealing tanks and armor plate, and their crews had orders to avoid flak at all costs. Many released their gliders too far offshore, and twenty of twenty-four failed to reach land. Jim Wallwork refused three release attempts until his tug was closer to shore, then survived a rough landing beside an Italian machine-gun position. News of the drownings led John Howard to increase swimming requirements for his men. Wallwork later returned to Britain for Operation Deadstick, carrying experience from the Sicily failure into the D-Day coup de main.

evidence.note: The reading recounts Waco glider training, disastrous offshore releases at Sicily, a pilot's landing, and his later participation in Operation Deadstick.

segments.summary: Stephen Ambrose's Pegasus Bridge links the famous D-Day coup de main to hard glider experience and lessons learned during the invasion of Sicily.

segments.title: Operation Chariot's dockyard assault teams
segments.body: The final selection turns to the St Nazaire Raid, also known as Operation Chariot. Roy's commando team disembarks from the destroyer's forecastle, supports a wounded sergeant, and moves through the dockyard using knowledge learned from a detailed model. Bamboo scaling ladders show how closely each party prepared for its assigned structures and obstacles. After German troops flee and a Tommy gun jams, the attackers use grenades to clear gun positions 64 and 65 on the pumping-station roof. They then demolish the abandoned weapons, completing their assigned task inside the larger dockyard assault. This ground-level episode presents the raid as a collection of rehearsed assault and demolition missions alongside the destroyer strike against the dry dock.

evidence.note: An account of the St Nazaire assault team locating, clearing, and demolishing dockyard gun positions.

segments.summary: C. E. Lucas Phillips's account of the St Nazaire Raid follows a commando team clearing and demolishing German gun positions beside the dock.
